145: T HE A CTOR . Wipe out half my debt.
144: K OSTILYOFF . How can I do that?
143: T HE A CTOR . Suppose you reward me right now?
141: K OSTILYOFF . In the Beyond, little brother—there all our deeds will be reckoned up.
138: K OSTILYOFF . You’re a kindly fellow. That’s good. Some day you’ll be rewarded for it.
137: T HE A CTOR . I’ve put her down in the hall and wrapped her up.
136: K OSTILYOFF [ with a start ] God, what a noise! [ The Actor enters. ]

133: K OSTILYOFF . Why should I choke you? What would be the use? God be with you—live and prosper! 131: K LESHTCH . You’ll put a noose around my neck and choke me . . . you’ll croak soon enough, and still all you think of is half rubles—

129: K LESHTCH . I didn’t see her.
127: K OSTILYOFF . I say, are you filing? [ Pause ] What did I want to ask? [ Quick and low ] Hasn’t my wife been here?
122: K OSTILYOFF . Pass on, please! [ Hums a religious tune, glances about him suspiciously, and bends his head to the left as if listening to what is happening in Pepel’s room. Kleshtch is jangling his keys and scraping away with his file, and looks askance at the other ] Filing?
121: T HE A CTOR . Step aside, you—don’t you see that we’re invalids?
120: K OSTILYOFF . Going for a stroll? What a nice couple—the gallant cavalier and the lady fair!
119: T HE A CTOR . If you wish, I’ll take you into the hallway. Get up, then, come! [ He helps her to rise, wraps some sort of a rag about her shoulders, and supports her toward the hall ] It isn’t easy. I’m sick myself—poisoned with alcohol . . . [ Kostilyoff appears in the doorway. ]
117: T HE A CTOR [ looks about him morosely, then goes to Anna ] Feeling bad, eh?
116: [ Anna coughs; Satine is lying down motionless, his hands folded behind his head. ]
115: B UBNOFF . They don’t only hit you over the head, but over the rest of the body as well. [ Rises ] I must go and buy some thread—our bosses are late to-day—seems as if they’ve croaked. [ Exit ]
114: S ATINE . My head buzzes—ah—why do people have to hit each other over the heads?
113: K LESHTCH [ morosely ] I don’t care who’s asking—
112: B UBNOFF [ unconcernedly ] I don’t care if you open the door—it’s your wife who’s asking—
111: K LESHTCH . All right. You’re sitting on the bunk, I on the floor. You change places with me, and I’ll let you open the door. I have a cold as it is.
110: B UBNOFF . Open the door into the hall.
109: K LESHTCH . What shall I do?
108: A NNA . Andrei Mitritch—I’m suffocating—I can’t breathe—
107: S ATINE . What are you cursing for? I know you haven’t a kopeck in the world!
106: K LESHTCH . Go to hell! All of you!

104: T HE A CTOR . I say—talent, that’s what you need to play heroes. And talent is nothing but faith in yourself, in your own powers—
103: B UBNOFF . I only have two—
102: S ATINE . Bubnoff, give me five kopecks.
101: T HE A CTOR [ sits, nursing his knees ] Education is all rot. Talent is the thing. I knew an actor—who read his parts by heart, syllable by syllable—but he played heroes in a way that . . . why—the whole theatre would rock with ecstasy!
99: B UBNOFF . Oh, well—just matching thoughts—no matter how much dye you get on yourself, it all comes off in the end—yes, yes—
98: S ATINE . What are you trying to prove?
96: S ATINE . Well, and what then?
94: B UBNOFF . I’ve heard it a hundred times. Well, so you were! That isn’t very important! Me—well—once I was a furrier. 93: S ATINE . I was. There are some excellent books—and lots of curious words . . . Once I was an educated man, do you know?
92: B UBNOFF . Were you really a telegrapher?
91: S ATINE . I love unintelligible, obsolete words. When I was a youngster—and worked as a telegraph operator—I read heaps of books. . . .
89: [ Back stage is heard a dull murmur, cries, and a police whistle. Kleshtch sits down to work, filing screechily. ]
88: T HE A CTOR . None of your business. [ Striking his chest ] Ophelia! O—remember me in thy prayers!
87: [ Kleshtch comes from the kitchen. ] K LESHTCH . Will you start playing with the broom?
86: T HE A CTOR . In Hamlet they say: “Words, words, words!” It’s a good play. I played the grave-digger in it once. . . .
85: B UBNOFF . Then why did you say it? S ATINE . Just so! I’m bored, brother, with human words—all our words. Bored! I’ve heard each one of them a thousand times surely.
83: B UBNOFF . What does it mean?
81: S ATINE . Words—and here’s another one for you—transcendentalistic . . .
80: B UBNOFF . What are you muttering?
78: T HE A CTOR [ shaking his fist at him ] Nonsense! I’m telling you seriously . . . if the organism is poisoned . . . that means it’s bad for me to sweep the floor—to inhale the dust . . .
76: T HE A CTOR [ stubbornly ] Not organon—organism!
74: T HE A CTOR [ loud, as if he had suddenly awakened ] Yesterday the doctor in the hospital said to me: “Your organism,” he said, “is entirely poisoned with alcohol . . .”
73: K LESHTCH [ walking away ] Never mind—maybe you’ll get well—you can never tell! [ Goes into kitchen ]
72: A NNA . Go and eat! It’s hard on me. . . . I suppose very soon . . .
71: K LESHTCH . Frightened, are you? Don’t be! You’ll get all right!
70: A NNA . No. Why should I eat? You’re a workman—you need it.
69: K LESHTCH [ coming over to her ] And you—don’t you want any?
68: A NNA . Kvashnya left me some dumplings over there—you eat them!
64: T HE A CTOR [ climbing down from the stove ] It’s bad for me to inhale dust. [ With pride ] My organism is poisoned with alcohol. [ Sits down on a bunk, meditating ]
63: K VASHNYA [ to Actor ] See to it that you sweep up! [ Crosses to outer door, letting the Baron pass ahead ]
62: S ATINE . It paid you to be born a Baron, eh?
61: [ The Baron comes from the kitchen, across his shoulders a wooden beam from which hang earthen pots covered with rags. ] T HE B ARON . Heavier than ever!
60: T HE A CTOR . It’s always I . . . I don’t understand why. . . .
59: K VASHNYA [ to the Baron through kitchen door ] Come on—you! They don’t need you! Actor! You were asked to do it, and now you go ahead and attend to it—it won’t kill you . . .
58: N ASTYA [ goes to kitchen ] Not so’s you’ll notice it!
57: T HE B ARON [ returning the book to her ] Nastya! Sweep the floor for me—will you?
56: N ASTYA [ getting up ] What do you want? Give it back to me! You scoundrel! And that’s a nobleman for you!
55: T HE B ARON . Go to blazes! Nastya will do it. Hey there—fatal love! Wake up! [ Takes the book away from Nastya ]
54: T HE A CTOR . That doesn’t concern me. Go to the gallows if you like. It’s your turn to sweep the floor just the same—I’m not going to do other people’s work . . .
53: [ The Baron comes from the kitchen. ] T HE B ARON . I’ve no time to clean . . . I’m going to market with Kvashnya.
52: T HE A CTOR . To hell with Vassilisa! To-day is the Baron’s turn to clean. . . . Baron!
51: K LESHTCH . Wait till Vassilisa comes—she’ll show you whose business it is!
50: T HE A CTOR . None of your business!
49: K LESHTCH . Say! You crawl from that stove—and start cleaning house! Don’t play the delicate primrose!
48: T HE A CTOR [ after a silence ] I don’t understand—
47: S ATINE . Because a man can die only once!
44: T HE A CTOR [ raising his head from the top of the stove ] One of these days they’ll beat you to death!
42: B UBNOFF . That’s why they beat you.
40: B UBNOFF . Were you playing cards?
39: S ATINE . Suppose they did—but why did they?
38: B UBNOFF . Does it make any difference who?
37: S ATINE [ sitting up in his bunk ] Who beat me up yesterday?
35: N ASTYA [ muttering ] Leave me alone—I don’t bother you . . .
34: T HE B ARON [ painfully pushing forward Nastya’s head ] Throw it away—little fool!
32: K VASHNYA . You must eat. Hot food—good for you! I’ll leave you some in a cup. Eat them when you feel like it. Come on, sir! [ To Kleshtch ] You evil spirit! [ Goes into kitchen ]
31: A NNA . No, thanks. Why should I eat?
30: K VASHNYA . We’ll go presently. [ To Anna ] Like some hot dumplings?
29: T HE B ARON . Kvashnya! Time to go to market. . . .
28: K VASHNYA . Well, well! You poor soul . . . how’s the pain in the chest—any better?
27: A NNA . Leave me alone—get away from me. . . .
26: K VASHNYA [ walking up to Anna ] Little mother, how did you ever manage to live with this wretch?
25: B UBNOFF . Noise won’t keep you from dying.
23: A NNA . Every blessed day . . . let me die in peace, can’t you?
22: A NNA [ putting her head through the curtains ] The day has started. For God’s sake, don’t row! K LESHTCH . Whining again!
21: N ASTYA [ without lifting her head ] Hey—go away!
20: T HE B ARON . They’re off again! Nastya, where are you?
19: K VASHNYA . Ho-ho! can’t stand the truth, can you?
18: K LESHTCH . Shut up, you old bitch! It’s none of your business!
17: K VASHNYA . Sure! Anything else? You nearly beat your wife to death!
16: K LESHTCH . Oh—what a great lady . . . but you’ll marry Abramka just the same—that’s all you’re waiting for . . .
15: N ASTYA [ reaching for the book ] Give it back!
14: T HE B ARON [ hitting Nastya on the head with the book ] Nastya, you little fool!
13: K VASHNYA [ to Kleshtch ] You crimson goat, you—calling me a liar! How dare you be so rude to me?
12: [ The Baron looks at her and waves the book in the air ]
11: N ASTYA [ stretching out her hand ] Give it back—give it back! Stop fooling!
10: T HE B ARON [ snatching the book out of Nastya’s hand and reading the title ] “Fatal Love” . . . [ Laughs ]
9: K LESHTCH . You lie! You’re going to marry Abramka. . . .
6: K VASHNYA . Why should I, said I, a free woman, my own mistress, enter my name into somebody else’s passport and sell myself into slavery—no! Why—I wouldn’t marry a man even if he were an American prince!
4: B UBNOFF [ to Satine ] What are you grunting about? [ Satine keeps on grunting ]
3: K VASHNYA . No, my dear, said I, keep away from me with such proposals. I’ve been through it all, you see—and not for a hundred baked lobsters would I marry again!
2: T HE B ARON . And then?
1: It is an early spring morning.
0: A cellar resembling a cave. The ceiling, which merges into stone walls, is low and grimy, and the plaster and paint are peeling off. There is a window, high up on the right wall, from which comes the light. The right corner, which constitutes Pepel’s room, is partitioned off by thin boards. Close to the corner of this room is Bubnoff’s wooden bunk. In the left corner stands a large Russian stove. In the stone wall, left, is a door leading to the kitchen where live Kvashnya, the Baron, and Nastya. Against the wall, between the stove and the door, is a large bed covered with dirty chintz. Bunks line the walls. In the foreground, by the left wall, is a block of wood with a vise and a small anvil fastened to it, and another smaller block of wood somewhat further towards the back. Kleshtch is seated on the smaller block, trying keys into old locks. At his feet are two large bundles of various keys, wired together, also a battered tin samovar, a hammer, and pincers. In the centre are a large table, two benches, and a stool, all of which are of dirty, unpainted wood. Behind the table Kvashnya is busying herself with the samovar. The Baron sits chewing a piece of black bread, and Nastya occupies the stool, leans her elbows on the table, and reads a tattered book. In the bed, behind curtains, Anna lies coughing. Bubnoff is seated on his bunk, attempting to shape a pair of old trousers with the help of an ancient hat shape which he holds between his knees. Scattered about him are pieces of buckram, oilcloth, and rags. Satine, just awakened, lies in his bunk, grunting. On top of the stove, the Actor, invisible to the audience, tosses about and coughs.
